Attention solution: attention lets the decoder dynamically focus on relevant input tokens instead of relying only on one compressed vector. Semantic search connection: modern semantic search also compares query/document representations in vector space, using learned similarity to retrieve by meaning. Implicit link: representation quality and relevance scoring moved from fixed compression toward dynamic or vector based matching.

Semantic search transforms information retrieval from pattern matching to meaning matching, representing a paradigm shift from syntactic to semantic understanding of queries and documents.

question: What role does negative transfer play in choosing between full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient methods like LoRA?
answer_key: Negative transfer occurs when source and target are dissimilar
PEFT methods like LoRA fine-tune fewer parameters, reducing the risk of overwriting general knowledge
model_answer: Negative transfer occurs when source and target tasks or domains are dissimilar, so transferred knowledge hurts performance. That makes full fine tuning riskier when the source and target are mismatched because the adaptation can push the model toward harmful source domain patterns. Parameter efficient methods such as LoRA keep pretrained weights frozen and learn low rank update matrices, so they adapt the model while changing only a small learned component.

7.1 Core Concept
LoRA hypothesizes that weight updates during fine-tuning have low intrinsic rank. Instead of updating full weight matrices, LoRA learns low-rank decomposition matrices that are added to frozen pretrained weights.

7.2 Mathematical Formulation
For a pretrained weight matrix W, LoRA learns matrices A and B such that the effective weight becomes W + BA, where B and A have much smaller dimensions than W.

7.3 Rank Selection
The rank r determines adapter capacity and parameter count. Lower ranks reduce parameters but limit expressivity. Typical values range from 4 to 64 depending on task complexity.

7.4 Target Layers
LoRA is typically applied to attention projection matrices (query, key, value, output). Applying to all linear layers increases capacity but also parameter count.

7.5 Merging
After training, LoRA weights can be merged into base weights (W_new = W + BA), eliminating inference overhead. This enables deployment without architectural changes.

7.6 Adoption
LoRA has become popular for fine-tuning large language models and text-to-image models like Stable Diffusion. Hugging Face's PEFT library provides standardized LoRA implementations.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate external information before generating responses. With RAG, LLMs consult specified document collections to supplement their pre-existing training knowledge.

RAG combines information retrieval with text generation. Rather than relying solely on parametric knowledge encoded during training, RAG systems access non-parametric knowledge stores at inference time. This hybrid approach provides dynamic access to current, domain-specific, or proprietary information.

The core insight is that generation quality improves when models can reference relevant source documents rather than relying entirely on compressed knowledge in weights. RAG trades off inference-time compute for improved accuracy and groundedness.

The term RAG was introduced in a 2020 research paper by Facebook AI Research (now Meta AI), establishing the paradigm of retrieval-augmented language models for knowledge-intensive tasks.

Fine-tuning in deep learning is the process of adapting a model trained for one task (the upstream task) to perform a different, usually more specific, task (the downstream task). It involves applying additional training to the parameters of a neural network that have been pre-trained.

Fine-tuning is a form of transfer learning that reuses knowledge learned from original training objectives. Rather than training from scratch, fine-tuning leverages pretrained representations as initialization, dramatically reducing data requirements and computational costs.

The core insight is that neural networks learn hierarchical representations during pretraining that transfer across tasks. Lower layers capture general features while higher layers capture task-specific patterns. Fine-tuning adapts these representations to new objectives.

Fine-tuning has become the dominant paradigm for deploying deep learning in practice. Pretrained models serve as foundation, with task-specific adaptation enabling practical applications without massive compute budgets.

A large language model (LLM) is a language model trained with self-supervised machine learning on vast amounts of text, designed for natural language processing tasks, especially language generation. The largest and most capable LLMs are generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs) that provide core capabilities for chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude.

LLMs consist of billions to trillions of parameters and operate as general-purpose sequence models capable of generating, summarizing, translating, and reasoning over text. They represent a significant technological advancement in their ability to generalize across tasks with minimal task-specific supervision.

These models acquire predictive power regarding syntax, semantics, and ontologies inherent in human language corpora, but also inherit inaccuracies and biases present in training data. LLMs can be fine-tuned for specific tasks or guided through prompt engineering.

In-context learning (ICL) is a paradigm that allows language models to learn tasks given only a few examples in the form of demonstration within the input prompt. The model reads training examples to understand input-output distributions and generates appropriate responses without any gradient updates or parameter changes.

Unlike traditional machine learning where models are limited to tasks their training was designed for, ICL enables models to acquire new skills simply by providing examples in the input. This represents a fundamental shift from weight-based learning to context-based learning.

ICL is training-free: the model uses only forward computation without backpropagation. Knowledge is conveyed through the prompt structure rather than through parameter updates. This makes ICL computationally efficient and enables instant skill acquisition.

The capability was first prominently observed in GPT-3 and has become a defining characteristic of large language models. ICL enables unprecedented versatility, allowing a single model to be deployed for diverse tasks by simply changing the prompt.

Fine-tuning in deep learning is the process of adapting a model trained for one task (the upstream task) to perform a different, usually more specific, task (the downstream task). It involves applying additional training to the parameters of a neural network that have been pre-trained.

Fine-tuning is a form of transfer learning that reuses knowledge learned from original training objectives. Rather than training from scratch, fine-tuning leverages pretrained representations as initialization, dramatically reducing data requirements and computational costs.

The core insight is that neural networks learn hierarchical representations during pretraining that transfer across tasks. Lower layers capture general features while higher layers capture task-specific patterns. Fine-tuning adapts these representations to new objectives.

Fine-tuning has become the dominant paradigm for deploying deep learning in practice. Pretrained models serve as foundation, with task-specific adaptation enabling practical applications without massive compute budgets.

8.1 Task Adaptation
Fine-tuning adapts the pre-trained model to specific downstream tasks. The pre-training task head is replaced with a task-appropriate output layer, and all model parameters (including pre-trained encoder weights) are updated on task-specific labeled data.

BERT requires minimal architectural modification for different tasks. The same pre-trained encoder serves as the foundation, with only the output layer varying by task type.

8.3 Sample Efficiency

8.4 Computational Efficiency
